q086.question: How can the player obtain the Moonlight Greatsword in each game where it appears, and what attributes or combat styles best support its use?
q086.answer: The Moonlight Greatsword is obtained differently in each game but is consistently an Intelligence-oriented greatsword. In Dark Souls it is cut from the tail of Seath the Scaleless, requiring 825 damage to a spot a bit above the tip of his tail; it deals pure Magic damage, raises magic defense by 40 points, cannot be Enchanted, and has 136% Intelligence scaling with 0% Strength, Dexterity and Faith, while its strong attack fires a magic projectile whose damage is based on the player's Intelligence. In Dark Souls II it is obtained by trading the Old Paledrake Soul to Weaponsmith Ornifex in NG+, with the Old Paledrake Soul coming from The Duke's Dear Freja in NG+ and beyond or through a Bonfire Ascetic in NG; the sword again deals pure Magic damage, scales strongly with Intelligence, and its strong attack launches a magic projectile at a cost of 10 durability, with a Faintstone infusion becoming worthwhile around 45 Intelligence and its low Strength and Dexterity requirements making it perfect for pure mage builds. In Dark Souls III it is obtained by transposing the Soul of Consumed Oceiros with Ludleth of Courland for 10,000 souls; unlike earlier versions it inflicts both physical and Magic damage and has poor Strength scaling, so the physical scaling should be ignored outside meeting minimum requirements in favor of leveling Intelligence, which only scales effectively up to 40. Its skill Moonlight Vortex charges a powerful thrust, fully charging either strong attack unleashes a moonlight wave at the cost of 4 durability, and the weapon is best utilized with heavy armor to make use of Poise.

q087.question: How does the Estus Flask work in Dark Souls, and where can the player find Fire Keeper Souls to increase its healing effectiveness?
q087.answer: In Dark Souls, the Estus Flask is the basic healing item and is replenished by resting at bonfires. An Estus flask is first granted by Oscar before he succumbs to death (or automatically if the player kills him); thereafter resting at an unkindled bonfire gives up to 5 Estus charges, a kindled bonfire gives 10, and further kindling through the Rite of Kindling adds 5 charges per kindle up to a maximum of 20. The amount each flask heals is upgraded by offering Fire Keeper Souls to other Fire Keepers, up to seven times, and only seven Fire Keeper Souls can be obtained in one game. Four are found in the world: in the Undead Parish on an altar in the Undead Church guarded by a Berenike Knight, in the New Londo Ruins on the right-hand side when crossing the narrow wooden walkway, in Blighttown in a waste-water pit reached after taking the wooden elevator, and in The Duke's Archives inside Big Hat Logan's prison. The other three are held by Fire Keepers and require killing them or otherwise obtaining their souls: Quelaag's Sister, the Darkmoon Knightess, and Anastacia of Astora's soul from Lautrec after he kills her. The typical use of a Fire Keeper Soul is to give it to one of the three Fire Keepers, Anastacia below Firelink Shrine, Quelaag's Sister in Quelaag's Domain, or the Darkmoon Knightess at the main bonfire in Anor Londo, which reinforces the Estus Flask and increases its healing power per charge. Consuming a Fire Keeper Soul from the inventory instead grants 5 units of liquid Humanity and restores full health, but this is not recommended unless the flask is already fully reinforced, and it is not possible to obtain +7 flasks in a single playthrough because reinforcing requires an active Fire Keeper.

claims.quote: An Estus flask is first granted to the player by Oscar before he succumbs to death. Alternately, the player automatically receives the Estus Flask if they kill Oscar. q088.question: What are the differences between the Covetous Silver Serpent Ring and Covetous Gold Serpent Ring, and how can the player obtain them?
q088.answer: The two rings serve different purposes: the Covetous Gold Serpent Ring boosts the wearer's Item Discovery so that more items can be amassed, while the Covetous Silver Serpent Ring rewards additional souls for each kill. The Gold ring increases Item Discovery by 200 and does not stack with the Symbol of Avarice; it is found in Sen's Fortress in a hidden room opened when boulders fill a deep pit at the end of a dead-end hallway, after which the fourth boulder destroys the wall, so the player should move out of the way after grabbing it because the boulders keep rolling. Item Discovery improves the chance for enemies to drop items and is a visible stat in Dark Souls with a base of 100 that can be raised up to 410 by special items; mechanically, increasing it divides the enemy's base number of empty drop-pool slots by Item Discovery/100 while leaving item slots unaffected. The Gold ring is invaluable for hunting upgrade materials and rare items such as the Channeler's Trident. The Silver ring grants an additional 20% souls for enemies killed and stacks and compounds with the Symbol of Avarice and overkilling for a total of 172.8% of the original souls, though overkill does not affect bosses; it is found in the Tomb of the Giants after the first fog gate, on a hidden optional path near a Brave Warrior corpse, reached by dropping off on the right side where Prism Stones can reveal the path, guarded by five Bone Towers that emerge when the ring is within reach.

claims.text: The Covetous Gold Serpent Ring is engraved with the serpent and boosts its wearer's item discovery, so that more items can be amassed.
claims.quote: This gold ring, engraved with the serpent, boosts its wearer's item discovery, so that more items can be amassed.

q089.question: How do the Ring of Favor and Protection, Havel's Ring, and Cloranthy Ring affect character performance, and what does the wiki recommend for builds that use them?
q089.answer: In Dark Souls, the Ring of Favor and Protection increases the player's maximum HP, Stamina and equipment load by 20% each, but the item is destroyed if it is ever removed, and after reaching 40 Endurance it is the only way to further increase maximum Stamina, allowing a total of 192 Stamina with 40 Endurance. Havel's Ring raises maximum equipment burden by 50% and is useful because it lets many classes upgrade from a slow roll to a mid roll or better, giving a wider range of equipment options without sacrificing mobility; later the player may want to invest in Endurance to free up the ring slot, though heavier weapon and armor users may need both the ring and high Endurance. The Cloranthy Ring increases stamina regeneration by 20 per second and stacks with other stamina-regenerating items such as Green Blossoms, the Grass Crest Shield and Power Within. Equipment load breakpoints are 25%, 50% and 100%: at 25% or below the player has fast sprint/walk speed and fast rolls, from 26% to 50% movement is medium with medium rolls, from 51% to 100% movement is slow with fat rolls and stamina regeneration is reduced by 20%, and above 100% the player cannot sprint or roll and regeneration is reduced by 30%. Maximum equip load equals 40 plus Endurance, and item modifiers stack multiplicatively (Mask of the Father 5%, Ring of Favor and Protection 20%, Havel's Ring 50%, for a total of 89% with all three). The wiki generally advises keeping equipment load at or below 25% in order to stay nimble.

q090.question: What are the effects of the different elemental infusions and resins in Dark Souls III, and when can a weapon be buffed with a temporary effect?
q090.answer: In Dark Souls III, infusion is a form of weapon reinforcement performed by Blacksmith Andre that changes a weapon's attributes; for example, the Blessed infusion increases Faith scaling while reducing scaling for every other parameter, and Blessed weapons gradually restore HP and deal bonus damage to reanimated foes. Fire Gems infuse a weapon with equally split physical and fire damage, remove all scaling effects, and are most efficient at minimum wielding requirements, though the player must contend with two defenses. Chaos Gems infuse Fire damage, add Intelligence and Faith scaling while reducing Strength and Dexterity scaling and base damage, and raise pre-existing Magic, Lightning and Dark scaling, with Fire scaling soft-capping at 30 Intelligence and 30 Faith. Lightning Gems infuse Lightning damage and Faith scaling while reducing Strength and Dexterity scaling and base damage, with scaling soft-capping at 40 Faith. Dark Gems infuse Dark damage, add Intelligence and Faith scaling while reducing Strength and Dexterity scaling and base damage, with scaling soft-capping at 30 Intelligence and 30 Faith. Temporary buffs come from consumable resins and spells: Charcoal Pine Resin applies 85 Fire damage to the right-hand weapon for 60 seconds, Gold Pine Resin adds 95 Lightning damage for 60 seconds, Lightning Blade adds 95% of the equipped talisman or sacred chime's Spell Buff as Lightning damage for 60 seconds, Dark Blade adds 85% of Spell Buff as Dark damage for 60 seconds, and Darkmoon Blade adds 95% as Magic damage for 60 seconds. Spell Buff is the stat on a catalyst that determines spell and weapon-buff effectiveness, scaling with Intelligence and Faith and dropping to a flat 60 if the catalyst's requirements are not met. Some weapons cannot be buffed or infused at all, such as the Chaos Blade.

Infusing a weapon can be performed by talking with Blacksmith Andre and change the attributes of a weapon. For example, infusing a Scimitar with the Blessed infusion increases the scaling on that weapon for Faith, while reducing scaling for every other parameter.

Many Undead enemies or creatures, such as Peasant Hollows and Starved Hounds, are naturally weak to Fire damage, and thus, a Fire-infused weapon can prove useful. However, one must be cautious, as attacking an enemy with such a weapon now has to take into account two defenses. As such, enemies that possess a resistance to fire will take notably less damage.

Fire infusions also remove *all* scaling effects present on the weapon after infusion, which means that it is most efficient when using such an infused weapon at its minimum wielding requirements

q091.question: How does the Covenant of Artorias differ from other rings, why is it required for a particular boss encounter, and what happens if the player removes it at the wrong time?
q091.answer: The Covenant of Artorias differs from most rings in that it has no purpose other than allowing its wearer, like Artorias himself, to traverse the Abyss, and it is one of the very few rings that do not carry over to NG+, so the player must kill Great Grey Wolf Sif every playthrough to obtain it. The ring is obtained by killing Sif, who can be found in Darkroot Garden behind large, glowing doors guarding the grave of Artorias the Abysswalker. It is required for the Four Kings encounter because the Abyss lies at the end of the New Londo Ruins, and without wearing the ring it is impossible to survive the fall into the Abyss, so the player cannot reach the Four Kings. Taking off the ring during the fight with the Four Kings will cause the player to be devoured by the Abyss. Once the Four Kings have been defeated, the Abyss ceases to kill the player in their world and the ring is no longer required to traverse it, although it is required again if the player is summoned as a phantom to help another player defeat the Four Kings. Dropping into the Abyss immediately triggers the Four Kings to spawn, and after they are defeated a bonfire appears.

q092.question: How do miracles such as Lightning Spear and Sunlight Spear differ in their requirements, damage, and acquisition methods?
q092.answer: In Dark Souls, almost every miracle has some level of Faith requirement, and Faith softcaps are 30/50; joining the Warrior of Sunlight covenant initially requires 25 Faith (50 in the pre-patch version), a requirement lowered by 5 for every boss the player helps another defeat as a white phantom. Joining the covenant grants the Lightning Spear miracle, and only one copy of Lightning Spear and its variants may be obtained regardless of playthrough. Lightning Spear has a lightning attack power equal to 2.7 times the talisman's magic adjust, with a long casting time, pinpoint accuracy, very long effective range, and scaling with Faith and the talisman used. Great Lightning Spear is obtained by reaching +1 rank in the Warrior of Sunlight covenant by offering ten Sunlight Medals; it is nearly identical to Lightning Spear but appears larger, deals more damage, and has attack power equal to 3.0 times the talisman's magic adjust. Sunlight Spear is a reward for offering the soul of Gwyn to the statue at the Sunlight Altar in the Undead Parish; most players can only obtain it in NG+, though it is possible in NG if given Gwyn's soul by a phantom, and it may only be obtained once per character. Sunlight Spear requires the user to be a Warrior of Sunlight to cast and requires 50 Faith, deals attack power equal to 3.7 times the talisman's magic adjust plus high Poise damage, and although it deals more damage than Great Lightning Spear it comes with half the casts and occupies two slots.

q093.question: What are the major differences between the three Dark Souls games' healing systems, and how do Estus Flask upgrades and additional healing items work in each game?
q093.answer: Each game builds its healing around Estus Flasks but differs in how charges and potency are upgraded and in the supporting items. In Dark Souls, Estus is replenished at bonfires; an unkindled bonfire gives up to 5 charges, kindling gives 10, and the Rite of Kindling adds 5 per kindle up to 20. The amount healed is upgraded by offering Fire Keeper Souls to Fire Keepers up to seven times, with only seven souls available per game. Divine Blessings fully restore HP and clear Bleed, Poison and Toxic buildup and contracted effects but not Curse, heal faster than Estus, cannot be blocked by Lloyd's Talismans, and are limited in quantity. In Dark Souls II, the Emerald Herald gives the player a single Estus Flask in Majula, and Estus Flask Shards brought to her increase the number of flasks up to 12; Sublime Bone Dust raises the healing by 50 HP each up to +5, with a +0 flask healing 550 and a +5 flask healing 800. Lifegems are the common alternative, restoring 500 HP over 11 seconds with a stackable effect that ends instantly at full health, but they cannot be used in PvP. Human Effigies reverse Hollowing, restore the health bar to maximum and allow summon signs to be seen, but unlike Humanity they cannot be used as healing items. In Dark Souls III, the player starts with three Estus charges and can pick up the Ashen Estus Flask for an overall total of four; Estus Shards brought to Blacksmith Andre raise the combined charges of the two flasks to a maximum of 15, and Undead Bone Shards burned at Firelink Shrine raise potency up to +10. The Ashen Estus Flask restores FP, shares charges with the normal Estus Flask, and its potency can be increased by 20% with the Ashen Estus Ring, while the Estus Ring increases HP recovered from Estus by 20%. Divine Blessings in Dark Souls III fully restore HP and cure Poison, Toxic, Bleed and Frost while reducing their buildup, but not Curse, and only one can be carried at a time.

q094.question: How do covenants differ in their multiplayer functions and rewards, and which covenants focus on cooperation, invasions, or defending specific areas?
q094.answer: Covenants across the series divide broadly into cooperation, invasion and area-defense roles, each with its own currency and rewards. The Warriors of Sunlight are a co-op-oriented Dark Souls covenant whose members cross over worlds to engage in jolly co-operation; joining grants the Lightning Spear miracle and the Praise the Sun gesture, and members use a golden summon sign and appear as gold phantoms, earning Sunlight Medals when bosses are defeated. The Darkwraiths are a Dark Souls PvP covenant that invades other worlds to steal humanity, granting a Dark Hand, allowing purchase of Cracked Red Eye Orbs, and awarding a Red Eye Orb at rank +1 and the Dark Set and Darksword at rank +2. The Blade of the Darkmoon in Dark Souls is a PvP covenant that hunts those who have sinned, giving members the Blue Eye Orb and Darkmoon Blade Covenant Ring and rewarding Souvenirs of Reprisal, with the Darkmoon Blade miracle usable only in the covenant and scaling from 1.8x to 2.1x magic adjust as the player ranks up. In Dark Souls II, the Bell Keepers are a PvP covenant devoted to protecting Belfry Luna and Belfry Sol; wearing the Bell Keeper's Seal automatically invades trespassers, a victory returns the member with a Titanite Chunk, and ranking up is the only way to obtain the Hidden Weapon sorcery. The Way of Blue in Dark Souls II is a protection covenant: when invaded by a Dark Spirit, its members receive help from an automatically summoned Blue Sentinel, though this is not useful for PvE because the sentinel cannot hurt enemies. In Dark Souls III, the Watchdogs of Farron queue to defend the Crucifixion Woods and Farron Keep, are summoned when an Embered host trespasses the upper swamp, and return with a Wolf's Blood Swordgrass after defeating the host. The Aldrich Faithful similarly defend Aldrich's territory in Irithyll from trespassers anywhere from the courtyard after Pontiff Sulyvahn up to the rotating stairway to Anor Londo, earning Human Dregs from defeated hosts. The Blade of the Darkmoon in Dark Souls III functions identically to the Blue Sentinels, being summoned to help Way of Blue members invaded by red or purple spirits and rewarded with Proofs of a Concord Kept, or a Proof of a Concord Well Kept if an Aldrich Faithful is slain. The Dark Souls III Way of Blue has no ranking system and no rewards aside from receiving aid while invaded.

Players in this covenant will have an easier time co-oping with other Warriors of Sunlight, as well as Princess's Guards and members of the Way of White covenant. Also, Warriors of Sunlight will have a golden summon sign instead of a regular white summon sign, and appear as gold phantoms instead of white phantoms.

q095.question: How does summoning work in the Dark Souls series, including the conditions for seeing summon signs, NPC summons, and restrictions on cooperative play?
q095.answer: Summoning is done through soapstones, and each game gates who can see and place signs differently. In Dark Souls, the White Sign Soapstone places a friendly sign and can be used online regardless of whether the user is hollowed or human, or whether they have personally defeated bosses; other players can only see white signs if their owners are within 10 levels plus or minus an additional 10% of the viewer's level (a level 100 player can summon levels 80-120), and being in NG or NG+ has no influence on this. Members of the Warriors of Sunlight use golden summon signs instead of white ones. The Red Sign Soapstone requires the user to be unhollowed to place or summon, allows duels for humanity and souls, and the host does not need the area boss alive; red phantoms summoned this way cannot be indicted. NPC summons use the same sign system and appear under their own quest conditions, such as Anri's and Horace's signs before the Deacons after exhausting their dialogue. In Dark Souls II, the White Sign Soapstone summons a phantom who, on success, becomes human and receives a Token of Fidelity, while Heirs of the Sun members use a golden sign and receive a Sunlight Medal instead. The Small White Sign Soapstone summons a shade with a normal 12.5-minute time limit that shrinks as enemies are killed, and shades cannot gain more than 7,000 souls from a boss and receive a Smooth & Silky Stone for fulfilling their duty. If all bosses in an area are defeated, the player may only summon Shades there until at least one boss is respawned, though their own signs are unaffected. In Dark Souls III, the White Sign Soapstone lays a sign that only a Host of Embers may interact with; password matchmaking bypasses normal rules, scaling a high-level phantom down but not scaling a lower-level phantom up when entering a higher-level host, and summoning a white phantom increases boss health, stacking linearly with multiple phantoms. Embers make the summoning signs of Unkindled visible and allow co-operation, but also attract invaders, while red signs remain visible even where the boss is defeated and whether or not the host has an active Ember.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, the White Sign Soapstone places a friendly summon sign, requires the player to be online, and may be used regardless of whether the user is hollowed or human or has personally defeated bosses.
claims.quote: Using the white sign soapstone causes the player to place a friendly summon sign on the ground, enabling other players to summon them for co-operative play. In order to use the soapstone, players must be online. White Sign Soapstones may be used regardless of whether the user is hollowed or in human form, or whether they had personally defeated bosses themselves.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, players can only see white summon signs if their owners are within 10 levels plus or minus an additional 10% of the viewer's level, and being in NG or NG+ has no influence on this.
claims.quote: Players can only see white summon signs if their owners are within 10 levels (+/- an additional 10% of their current character level). For example, a level 100 player can choose to summon anyone between level 80 and level 120, and a level 30 player can choose to summon anyone between levels 17-43. Being in NG or NG+ has no influence on this (players in NG can summon others in NG+ and vice versa).

claims.text: In Dark Souls, the Red Sign Soapstone requires players to be unhollowed to place it or summon from it, allows duels for humanity and souls, and does not require the host's area boss to be alive; red phantoms summoned this way cannot be indicted.

Player placing soapstone may be summoned by players that are within range and (- (10 +10% of the placing player's level), or any level higher (for example, a level 100 player can be summoned by any player that is level 80 or higher); in addition, the host does not need the area boss to be alive to summon. People who share similar soul levels have a higher priority in match-making.

claims.text: Members of the Warrior of Sunlight covenant have golden summon signs instead of the standard white ones.
claims.quote: Members of the Warrior of Sunlight covenant have golden summon signs instead of the standard white ones.

claims.quote:
If successful when using a White Sign Soapstone in another player's world, the player will become human and be rewarded with a Token of Fidelity.
As a phantom, the player will dull in color over time, until they're disconnected from the host.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, a Shade summoned with the Small White Sign Soapstone has a normal time limit of 12 and a half minutes in the world, reduced as more enemies are killed.
claims.quote: The Shade summoned with a Small White Sign Soapstone will have a normal time limit of 12 and a half minutes in the world. This time limit will be reduced as more enemies are killed, regardless of whether they're killed by the host or the shade.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, if all bosses in an area are defeated, the player may only summon Shades in that area until at least one boss is respawned, while their own signs are unaffected.
claims.quote: If all bosses in an area are defeated, the player may only summon Shades in that area, until at least one boss is respawned. Their own signs are unaffected by this.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, the White Sign Soapstone lays a white summon sign on the ground that a Host of Embers may interact with to summon the sign's owner.

q096.question: What is the difference between parrying, backstabbing, and guard breaking, and which enemy attacks or weapon types can be countered with each technique?
q096.answer: Parrying, backstabbing and guard breaking are three different ways to open an enemy to critical damage. A backstab is performed by positioning behind a humanoid enemy on roughly the same level surface and doing a light attack with the shield down; it can be done with nearly every weapon except bows, crossbows, catalysts, talismans, pyromancy flames, whips and shields, deals high damage based on the weapon and its critical rate, cannot be interrupted, and grants invincibility frames during the animation (except in Dark Souls II, where damage is merely reduced). Most humanoid enemies can be backstabbed, and most enemies that can be parried and riposted can also be backstabbed, while non-humanoid enemies generally cannot. A parry is performed from the front with a left-handed weapon or shield's strong attack, deflecting an incoming attack and stunning the enemy; immediately after, a light attack performs a riposte, which deals extremely high damage based on weapon base damage and critical rate, even more than a backstab, and cannot be interrupted. In Dark Souls, shields cannot riposte, and bows, crossbows, talismans, catalysts, pyromancy flames, whips and shields cannot riposte. In Dark Souls II, the guard break replaces the kick: after a short windup the player delivers a backhand attack that stuns the target, and if the target's shield is up their guard is broken and they are stunned long enough for a Frontal Riposte. Dark Souls II parry timing must begin when a fast or medium weapon's attack animation starts, or mid-swing for slow weapons, whereas Dark Souls parries are performed near the end of the animation. Ripostes in Dark Souls II become available after a parry or guard break, bosses cannot be riposted, and there are standing, ground and frontal ripostes. Dark Souls II cannot parry jumping attacks except Reapers, or standing two-handed light and heavy attacks from greataxes, great hammers, ultra greatswords and curved greatswords. In Dark Souls III, parrying is executed with the left strong attack of a shield with the Parry skill or a specific weapon, and a riposte follows either a parry or a poise break; any Ultra Greatsword, Greataxe or Great Hammer used two-handed cannot be parried except on rolling and running attacks, nor can whips, ranged weapons, catalysts or shields.

claims.text: A backstab is performed by positioning behind a humanoid enemy on roughly the same level surface and doing a light attack with the shield down, and can be performed with nearly every type of weapon though exceptions exist.
claims.quote: Players may perform a backstab if they position themselves behind a humanoid enemy and do a light attack with shield down. Enemies must be on roughly the same level surface as the player. Backstabs can be performed with nearly every type of weapon, although exceptions exist (see below).

claims.text: Backstabs deal high damage based on the weapon and its critical rate, cannot be interrupted, and grant invincibility frames to both attacker and victim, except in Dark Souls II where damage can still be taken but is reduced.
claims.quote:
Backstabs deal high damage based on the damage of the weapon and its critical rate.

Backstabs cannot be interrupted. While in the motion of backstabbing, both the perpetrator and the victim are granted invincibility frames and cannot take further damage except for damage-over-time effects such as being poisoned, under the effects of toxic, or while using Power Within. An exception to invincibility frames is *Dark Souls II*, where you can still take damage during a backstab although the damage is reduced.

claims.text: Most humanoid enemies can be backstabbed and most enemies that can be parried and riposted can also be backstabbed, while non-humanoid enemies are generally impossible to backstab.
claims.quote: Most humanoid enemies can be backstabbed. Most enemies that can be parried and riposted can also be backstabbed. Some non-humanoid enemies, such as the Fang Boar in the Undead Parish (but not the ones in Anor Londo), can also be backstabbed, but generally non-humanoid enemies are impossible to backstab.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, a parry is performed from directly in front of a parryable enemy by using the left-handed weapon or shield's strong attack as the enemy attacks, deflecting it and stunning the enemy, after which a light attack executes a riposte.
claims.quote: Players may perform a parry and riposte by first positioning themselves directly in front of a parryable enemy. As the enemy attacks, players may parry with their left-handed weapon or shield (the left-handed strong attack), deflecting their attack, and thus executing the parry. Enemies are momentarily stunned after this. Immediately after, the player can perform a light attack to execute a riposte.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, ripostes deal extremely high damage based on weapon base damage and critical rate, even more than a backstab, and cannot be interrupted; the player has about one second after a parry to execute the riposte.
claims.quote:
The riposte is a special attack executed directly after a parry, an execution move that deals extremely high damage (even more damage than a backstab). Ripostes deal high damage based on the base damage of the weapon and its critical rate. Certain weapon types, such as daggers, have higher critical rates than other weapons. Thrusting Swords have higher [https://darksouls.fandom.com/wiki/Damage_(Dark_Souls)#Motion_Values Motion Values] on criticals that allow them to deal more damage with ripostes than what their critical rate and damage statistics would suggest. Wearing the Hornet Ring increases the damage dealt by ripostes, and (in some cases) changes the animation.

After executing a parry successfully, players have about one second to do the Riposte. During this time, they can also move or switch weapons, and still execute the Riposte successfully.

Ripostes cannot be interrupted. While in the motion of riposting, both the perpetrator and the victim are granted invincibility frames and cannot take further damage except for damage-over time effects such as being poisoned, under the effects of toxic, or while using Power Within.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, shields cannot perform ripostes, and bows, crossbows, talismans, catalysts, pyromancy flames, whips and shields cannot riposte.
claims.quote:
Bows
Crossbows
Talismans
Catalysts
Pyromancy Flame
Whips
Shields

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, the Guard Break replaces the kick: after a short windup the player delivers a backhand attack that stuns the target, and if the target's shield is up their guard is broken and they are stunned long enough for a Frontal Riposte.
claims.quote: The Guard Break move replaces the kick from *Dark Souls*. After a short windup, the player delivers a backhand attack, stunning their target. If the target's shield is up, their guard is broken: they are stunned for a longer period of time, during which the player can perform a Frontal Riposte on them.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, parry timing must be initiated when a fast or medium weapon's attack animation begins, or mid-swing for slow weapons, whereas Dark Souls parries are performed near the end of the animation.
claims.quote: The timing of a parry in *Dark Souls II* is different: it must be initiated when the enemy's attack animation begins, if parrying fast and medium weapons (daggers, straight swords, curved swords, etc.) or mid-swing, if parrying slow weapons (ultra greatswords, great hammers, etc.). In *Dark Souls*, parry had to be performed near the end of the animation (this difference, however, may not be very noticeable, it's more of a matter of personal preference).

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, ripostes become available after parrying an attack or guard breaking an enemy with their shield up, and bosses cannot be riposted.
claims.quote: Ripostes are special attacks that deal critical damage to enemies, they become available after Parrying an attack or Guard Breaking an enemy that has their shield up. Bosses cannot be Riposted.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, most weapon attacks can be parried except jumping attacks (excluding Reapers).
claims.quote: In most cases, all weapon's attacks can be parried, except jumping attacks (excluding Reapers).

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, a parry is executed with the left strong attack of a shield with the Parry skill or a specific weapon, and a riposte can follow a parry or, in some cases, a poise break.
claims.quote:
A **Parry** is executed by pressing the **Left Strong Attack** button ( / ) with a shield that has the "Parry" skill or specific weapon. Shields that can parry will have a small circular icon depicting a shield in the lower corner. There are generally 3 various parrying types: Fast, Normal, Special (Long). Some Katanas have the shortest recovery while some medium shields and curved swords will have a normal parry type. Specific shields have a longer "parry window", such as the Buckler or the Target Shield.

A **Riposte** can be executed after a parry, or in some cases after the enemy's poise is broken, to deal critical damage.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, any Ultra Greatsword, Greataxe or Great Hammer used two-handed cannot be parried, except for rolling and running attacks, nor can whips, ranged weapons, catalysts or shields.
claims.quote:
Any Ultra Greatsword, Greataxe, or Great Hammer two-handed (exceptions for rolling and running attacks)
Whips
Any ranged weapon

q097.question: How does New Game Plus change enemy difficulty, item availability, and rewards, and what does the wiki recommend completing before the next cycle?
q097.answer: New Game Plus restarts the world at higher difficulty while retaining most character progress, and each game handles the transition and its losses differently. In Dark Souls, NG+ starts automatically after defeating Gwyn and watching an ending; the story is identical, but NPCs and bosses have their stats multiplied (early areas receive larger multipliers), rewards in souls increase, and the player keeps all non-story weapons, armor, items and rings, with kindled bonfires remaining kindled. Before entering, players should account for the items that are lost: the Orange Charred Ring, the Covenant of Artorias, all key items including Embers, the Rite of Kindling, both Smithboxes, the Lordvessel and the Crest of Artorias, while only the Master Key and Bottomless Box are kept. Difficulty stops increasing past NG+7. In Dark Souls II, NG+ can be entered at any time from the Far Fire bonfire after an ending; the player keeps weapons, armor, rings, consumables, soul level, stats and covenant standings, but most key items, Fragrant Branches of Yore, the Key to the Embedded and the King's Ring are lost. NG+ introduces new black phantom enemies, changes some corpse and chest contents, adds boss drops, and changes some fights with new mechanics or enemies; enemy damage rises two to four times, souls rise similarly, health is usually doubled, and difficulty stops increasing at NG+7. A Bonfire Ascetic can raise one bonfire area to the next playthrough level without entering NG+, restoring most items (but not metal chests), though it is irreversible and persists into future playthroughs. In Dark Souls III, NG+ is offered after defeating the Soul of Cinder and choosing an ending, but can be declined and entered later from Firelink Shrine; entering immediately prevents access to events that only occur after the Soul of Cinder's defeat, such as Yuria of Londor leaving her armor and weapon after the Usurpation of Fire ending. NG+ resets the world while keeping non-story equipment, levels, stats and covenants, increases enemy health and damage while increasing souls, lets bosses drop their souls again for missing transpositions, and adds stronger ring versions on corpses in NG+ and NG+2; difficulty stops increasing at NG+6. All key items except the Champion's Bones are lost entering NG+.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, New Game Plus starts automatically after defeating Gwyn, Lord of Cinder and watching an ending, the story is identical, and difficulty stops increasing past NG+7.
claims.quote: New Game Plus starts automatically after completing the game by defeating Gwyn, Lord of Cinder and watching one of the endings. Completing the game again in New Game Plus or any subsequent iteration starts a new iteration, commonly referred to as New Game++ (NG+2), New Game+++ (NG+3) and so on. While the game allows for infinite iterations, difficulty stops increasing past NG+7.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, the primary difference in NG+ is increased difficulty through more powerful enemies and greater soul rewards, while the player keeps non-story weapons, armor, items and rings, and kindled bonfires remain kindled.
claims.quote: The story and events in New Game+ are identical to New Game. The primary difference is an increase in game difficulty, in the form of more powerful enemies, and greater reward in souls for their defeat. The player keeps all non-story based acquired weapons, armor, items, and rings. Additionally, bonfires kindled in New Game remain kindled in New Game+.

claims.text: In Dark Souls, entering NG+ loses the Orange Charred Ring, the Covenant of Artorias, and all key items including Embers, the Rite of Kindling, the Weapon Smithbox, Armor Smithbox, Repairbox, the Lordvessel and the Crest of Artorias, while the Master Key and Bottomless Box are kept.
claims.quote:
The Orange Charred Ring.
The Covenant of Artorias.
All Keys and items that appear under Keys in-game, including Embers, the Rite of Kindling, Weapon Smithbox, Armor Smithbox, Repairbox, the Lordvessel and the Crest of Artorias.

Exceptions are the Master Key and the Bottomless Box, which are not lost.

claims.text: In Dark Souls NG+, enemy difficulty is raised by applying a multiplier to all NPC and boss stats that varies by location, with early-game areas generally receiving a greater multiplier than late-game areas.
claims.quote: In New Game Plus, the game increases the difficulty by raising the stats of all NPCs (non-player characters, including enemies and bosses). Each NPC's new stats are determined by applying a multiplier to their base stats that varies depending on their location in the game world. As a general rule, NPCs in early-game areas have a greater

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, upon receiving an ending, NG+ can be entered at any time from the Far Fire bonfire in Majula.
claims.quote: Upon receiving an ending, NG+ can be entered at any time from the Far Fire bonfire in Majula.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, NG+ introduces new enemies, often black phantom versions of existing enemies, changes some corpse and chest contents, gives certain bosses additional drops, and changes some fights with new mechanics, attacks or additional enemies.
claims.quote: The primary differences are an increase in game difficulty, in the form of more powerful enemies, and greater soul gains from defeating these stronger enemies. New enemies are also introduced, often in the form of black phantom versions of enemies that normally appear in that area. Additionally, some corpses and chests contain different items, certain bosses gain additional drops, and some fights are changed through the addition of new mechanics, attacks, or additional enemies.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II NG+, enemies gain two, three or four times the damage, souls granted are increased by a similar amount, health is usually doubled, and difficulty stops increasing at New Game+7.
claims.quote: Upon entering New Game+, enemies gain two, three, or four times the damage and the souls they grant on death are increased by a similar amount, while health is usually doubled. On later New Game cycles, the increase is minute, and new enemies are only added in specific spots, such as the basement of the mansion in Majula. The difficulty stops increasing at New Game+7.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, burning a Bonfire Ascetic changes the entire bonfire area to the next playthrough level, restoring most items but not metal chests, and the effect is irreversible and persists on following playthroughs.
claims.quote: When burned, a Bonfire Ascetic will change the entire bonfire area to the next playthrough level. For example, if used during the first playthrough, it will bump the difficulty to New Game+, and if used at New Game++, it will bump the difficulty to New Game+++. This process is irreversible and persists on following playthroughs.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, NG+ is offered after defeating the Soul of Cinder and choosing an ending, can be declined, and can then be entered at any time from Firelink Shrine's bonfire.
claims.quote: Upon defeating the Soul of Cinder and choosing an ending, the player will be offered to enter New Game+. If they decline, they will arrive back at Firelink Shrine and will be free to continue exploring the game as normal. New Game+ can then be entered at any time from Firelink Shrine's bonfire.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, immediately entering NG+ prevents access to events that only occur after the defeat of the Soul of Cinder, such as Yuria of Londor leaving her armor set and weapon for the player to collect after the Usurpation of Fire ending.
claims.quote: Note that immediately entering the next New Game+ cycle will prevent the player from accessing events that only occur after the defeat of the Soul of Cinder, such as Yuria of Londor leaving her armor set and weapon for the player to collect following the Usurpation of Fire ending.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III NG+, enemies receive a substantial increase to health and damage but reward more souls, bosses drop their specific souls again so missed transposition items can be obtained, and stronger ring versions appear on corpses in NG+ and NG+2.
claims.quote:
Upon entering New Game+, enemies receive a substantial increase to their health and damage output, but also reward more souls upon their defeat. Furthermore, Bosses will drop their specific souls when killed, allowing the player to either transpose the items they did not obtain in their first New Game cycle, or duplicates of items they already obtained. This notably allows a player to transpose the Twin Princes' Greatsword without having another player drop one of the swords during online play.

More powerful versions of certain rings can be found as loot on corpses in New Game+. Further additions may be found on the third cycle, New Game+2. These additional rings continue to appear in every future New Game+ cycle, and as such can be collected in any cycle beyond the one they first appear in.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III, all key items except the Champion's Bones are lost upon entering NG+.
claims.quote: All key items, except for the Champion's Bones, are lost upon entering New Game+. As Dark Sigils are lost, the player's Hollowing stat will not increase until the sigils are obtained again, though the Hollowing level itself is unaffected by starting New Game+.

q098.question: How do the three Dark Souls games portray dragons and their relationship with the ancient world, and how do Seath, the Ancient Dragon, and the Nameless King fit into that history?
q098.answer: The series portrays dragons as remnants of the age before the First Flame, when the world was composed only of grey rocks, and their history is defined by betrayal, war, and attempts to reclaim or worship their power. In Dark Souls, Seath is one of the primordial archdragons, but he was born without the rock scales that made his brethren immortal and his pale body was infused with the magical power of moonlight; he betrayed his race to ally with Gwyn and the Lords, was instrumental in their victory, and helped exterminate much of the Ancient Dragons, afterwards pillaging their sacred Primordial Crystal. As a reward Seath was wed into Gwyn's family, made a Duke, given a fragment of Gwyn's Lord Soul and the Royal Archives, and used the Primordial Crystal to become immortal. The Stone Dragon, also called the Everlasting Dragon, is one of the few dragons left in the world and a descendant of the Everlasting Dragons, residing in the secluded Ash Lake and initiating players into the Path of the Dragon; the ancient dragons are described as half-living, half-element beings that do not feel pain. In Dark Souls II, the Ancient Dragon dwelling atop the Dragon Shrine is a mysterious, telepathic optional boss that is neutral until attacked and gives the Bearer of the Curse the Ashen Mist Heart, which allows entry into the memories of the dead. Its origins are doubtful: using the heart in Freja's arena reveals the memory of an Ancient Dragon and its soul, while the dragon atop the Shrine instead drops a Soul of a Giant, and Nashandra calls it a false deity and a prop while Sweet Shalquoir suggests it may be something merely playing the part of a dragon, perhaps tied to rumors that Lord Aldia tried to create a dragon. In Dark Souls III, the Nameless King was once a dragon-slaying god of war, the firstborn of Gwyn, who fought the dragons alongside Ornstein and his father with lightning spears and distinguished himself as a dragon slayer. After Gwyn linked the First Flame he inherited the sunlight and the crown, but his reign was marked by catastrophes, and he eventually sacrificed everything to ally himself with the ancient dragons; the other deities saw this as an unforgivable sin, dethroned and exiled him, stripped his deific status, destroyed his statues and erased his name from history, and he left his sunlight blade and ring on Gwyn's empty tomb as a final farewell. Archdragon Peak, where he is fought, was seemingly built as a shrine by the Man Serpents, descendants of the Ancient Dragons, to worship them.

claims.text: Seath is one of the primordial archdragons who inhabited the world before the First Flame, when the world was composed only of grey rocks; he was born without the rock scales that made his brethren immortal, and his pale deformed body was infused with the magical power of moonlight.
claims.quote:
Seath is one of the primordial archdragons who inhabited the world when, before the appearance of the First Flame, the world was composed only of grey rocks.

Seath was born with unique characteristics compared to the other archdragons, lacking the rock scales that made his brethren immortal. In addition, Seath's pale and deformed body was infused with the magical power of moonlight, through the study of which he created weapons that catalyzed it.

claims.text: Seath betrayed his race to ally with Gwyn and the Lords in their war against the dragons, was instrumental in their eventual victory, and the triumphant Lords exterminated much of the Ancient Dragons; Seath also pillaged their sacred Primordial Crystal.
claims.quote: At some point, the Four Lords who had found immense Lord Souls and built their civilizations underground emerged to the surface with the intention of waging war against the Dragons and conquering the world for themselves. Seath decided to betray his race to ally with Gwyn, Lord of Sunlight, and help the Lords in the war. He was instrumental in the gods' eventual victory, and the triumphant Lords would exterminate much of the Ancient Dragons, cementing their rule. Seath would also pillage the Ancient Dragons' sacred treasure, the Primordial Crystal, the centerpiece of his efforts to achieve immortality.

claims.text: Seath was wed into Gwyn's family as his son-in-law and made a Duke, and Gwyn gave him a fragment of his Lord Soul and the Royal Archives, a library that became known as The Duke's Archives.
claims.quote: Through their successful alliance against the Everlasting Dragons, Seath became a close friend to the Lord of Sunlight and was amply rewarded for his indispensable contributions to the war. He was wed into Gwyn's family as his son-in-law, inducting him into the nobility of the Gods, and was bestowed the honorific of "Duke". Gwyn further gifted Seath a fragment of his powerful Lord Soul and the Royal Archives, an enormous library towering above Anor Londo, which contained all the knowledge available to the city of the gods, leaving the dragon the freedom to do his own research; in time, the archives became so synonymous with Seath that they became known as "The Duke's Archives" instead.

claims.text: The Stone Dragon, also known as the Everlasting Dragon, is one of the few dragons left in the world, a descendant of the Everlasting Dragons, residing in the secluded Ash Lake and initiating the player into the Path of the Dragon covenant.
claims.quote: The Stone Dragon is one of the few dragons left in the world, descendant of the Everlasting Dragons. It resides itself in the incredibly secluded and mysterious location of Ash Lake.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, the Ancient Dragon is a massive dragon that speaks telepathically and is neutral to the player until attacked a couple of times; speaking to it gives the Ashen Mist Heart, which allows the player to cross into the memories of the dead.
claims.quote:
The Ancient Dragon is a massive dragon that speaks telepathically to the player. It is neutral to the player until it is attacked a couple of times.

Speaking to the Ancient Dragon will give the player the Ashen Mist Heart, an object allowing the player to cross into the memories of the dead.

claims.text: Little is known of the Ancient Dragon atop the Dragon Shrine, and the Ashen Mist Heart casts doubt on its identity: Nashandra calls it a false deity and a prop, Sweet Shalquoir implies it may be something playing the part of a dragon, and rumors suggest Lord Aldia tried to create a dragon.
claims.quote:
Little is known of the mysterious dragon dwelling atop the Dragon Shrine. It offers the Bearer of the Curse the Ashen Mist Heart, allowing them to peer into the memories of things long deceased. Ironically, this very item casts doubts about the dragon's true identity and origins. It can be used in Freja's arena to enter the memory of an Ancient Dragon, where one can find the dragon's soul. The Ancient Dragon atop the Shrine however, upon defeat, will drop a Soul of a Giant.

Further doubts surrounding the dragon's origins are raised by Nashandra and Sweet Shalquoir. Nashandra refers to the dragon as a *"false deity"* and a *"prop"*. Sweet Shalquoir claims there is *"A great creature far to the east. A colossal thing, with the strength to match its size. Or something playing the part at least."* This suggests that the Ancient Dragon is not a true dragon.

Rumors abound in Drangleic about the king's brother, Lord Aldia, who tried to create a dragon. Perhaps the existence of the Ancient Dragon, and its dubious origins, are testament to his success.

claims.text: The Nameless King was once a dragon-slaying god of war, before he sacrificed everything to ally himself with the ancient dragons.
claims.quote: The Nameless King was once a dragon-slaying god of war, before he sacrificed everything to ally himself with the ancient dragons.

claims.text: The Nameless King is the firstborn child of Gwyn and was worshipped as the god of war; during the war against the Dragons he fought alongside Dragon Slayer Ornstein and Gwyn, used sunlight to create lightning spears and infuse his weapons to damage dragon scales, and distinguished himself as a dragon slayer.
claims.quote:
The Nameless King is the firstborn child of Gwyn, Lord of Sunlight and one of the deities who resided in Anor Londo during the Age of Fire. He was worshipped by humans as the "god of war".

During the war against the Dragons, the eldest son took part in the fighting together with Dragon Slayer Ornstein and his father Gwyn, using sunlight like him to create lightning spears and infuse his weapons to damage the creatures' scales. The god of war distinguished himself as a dragon slayer, using his swordspear imbued with lightning and even creating his personal armor with the scales of his preys.

claims.text: After Gwyn linked the First Flame, the Nameless King inherited the sunlight and crown of his father, and was said to be inferior to none in military strength.
claims.quote: After his father Gwyn left to link the First Flame, the throne of Anor Londo would pass to the eldest son of the King; and so the Nameless King inherited the Sunlight of his father. He would thus wear the golden crown, and succeed his father's titles of "king of the gods" and "god of the sun". The Nameless King was said to be inferior to none in terms of military strength.

claims.text: The Nameless King eventually decided to sacrifice everything to ally himself with the dragons, which the other deities saw as an unforgivable sin; he was dethroned and exiled, deprived of deific status, his statues destroyed and his name erased, and he left his sunlight blade and ring on Gwyn's empty tomb.
claims.quote: The eldest son of Gwyn eventually decided to "sacrifice everything" to ally himself with the dragons. In the eyes of the other deities of Anor Londo, archenemies of the dragons, his actions amounted to an unforgivable sin; he was therefore dethroned and exiled from the city. The former king was deprived of his deific status, his statues destroyed and his name erased from the annals of history. Before leaving Anor Londo, the eldest left his sunlight blade miracle and ring on Gwyn's empty tomb in his mausoleum as a final farewell, still paying respects for his father.

claims.text: Archdragon Peak is populated by Man Serpents and Rock Lizards and was seemingly built as a shrine to worship the Ancient Dragons by their descendants, the Man Serpents.
claims.quote: Archdragon Peak is populated by Man Serpents and Rock Lizards. It was seemingly built as a shrine to worship the Ancient Dragons by their descendants, the Man Serpents.

claims.text: According to an interview with Miyazaki, the Stone Dragon does not feel pain when its tail is cut off because the ancient dragons are half-living, half-element beings that do not feel pain.
claims.quote: According to an interview with Miyazaki, the Stone Dragon does not feel pain when its tail is cut off. The ancient dragons are half-living, half-element, and do not feel pain.

q099.question: How does the Ringed City DLC expand the lore of the Pygmies and the Dark Soul, and why is the blood of the Dark Soul important to the Painter?
q099.answer: The Ringed City DLC expands the lore of the Pygmies by showing the city that Gwyn gave them at the edge of the world, where the Dark Soul was kept contained and the last daughter of Gwyn, Filianore, was left as a gift and worshipped as a goddess. The Ringed City is said to be located at world's end; despite the First Flame fading, a sun still hangs in the sky, and the cathedral at the city's center protects Filianore's sleep while hiding the Dark Soul. Filianore is the last daughter of Gwyn, who after winning the war against the dragons gave her to the Pygmy Lords together with a magnificent ringed city at the edge of the world and promised to return for her; the Pygmy Lords, who directly inherited the Dark Soul and protected it within themselves, were related to the Furtive Pygmy and ruled the city, relying on Filianore for salvation. At some point Filianore fell into a deep sleep hugging a Vagrant egg, creating a space-time barrier that isolated the city from the fading of the First Flame and kept the Dark at bay; the Spears of the Church were founded to protect her slumber and contain the Dark Soul. Slave Knight Gael sought the blood of the Dark Soul as pigment for the Painted World, knowing he was no Champion, that the Dark Soul would likely ruin him and that he had little hope of returning safely; he devoured the Pygmy Lords and their blood rich with the Dark Soul. The Painter, a young woman with draconic lineage whose mother taught her about the First Flame and the Dark Soul and who has the ability to create new Painted Worlds, is waiting for a pigment colored like the dark soul of man. After Gael's death the Ashen One receives the Blood of the Dark Soul, the pigment consisting of dark souls consumed by Gael with blood seeping from his body, and giving it to the Painter, now possessing both Flame and Dark, finally lets her begin painting a cold, dark and very gentle place.

claims.text: The Ringed City is said to be located at world's end; despite the First Flame fading there is still a sun in the sky, and the cathedral at the centre of the city protects the sleep of Princess Filianore and hides the Dark Soul.
claims.quote:
The Ringed City is said to be located at world's end. Despite the First Flame fading, there is still a sun in the sky.
The cathedral at the centre of the city protects the sleep of Princess Filianore and hides the Dark Soul.

claims.text: Filianore is the last daughter of Gwyn; after winning the war against the dragons, Gwyn gave her to the Pygmy Lords together with a magnificent ringed city at the edge of the world, promising he would return for her some day.
claims.quote:
Filianore is the last daughter of Gwyn, Lord of Sunlight. Her sacred symbol is a crest of young grass.

She did not reside in Anor Londo during the Age of Fire unlike the other deities. Her father Gwyn, after winning the war against the dragons, "gave" Filianore as a gift to the Pygmy Lords together with a magnificent ringed city at the edge of the world. Before leaving her in the Ringed City, Gwyn promised her that he would come back for her some day.

claims.text: The Pygmy Lords directly inherited the Dark Soul and protected it within themselves, being related to the Furtive Pygmy; Gwyn gifted them the city as a peace offering along with his daughter Filianore, and they ruled the city.
claims.quote:
This Pygmy Lord is a member of the royalty within the Ringed City, who directly inherited the Dark Soul and protected it within themselves, being related to the Furtive Pygmy in some way.

Lord Gwyn gifted them the city as a sort of peace offering, as well as his daughter Filianore, who would eventually slumber, preserving the city and keeping the Dark at bay. They ruled the city in a rather adequate manner, with the exception of a madman who would rise among the royalty.

claims.text: Filianore fell into a deep sleep hugging a Vagrant egg, creating a space-time barrier that isolated the Ringed City from the fading of the First Flame and kept the Dark Soul contained; the Spears of the Church were founded to protect her slumber and maintain the city's isolation.
claims.quote: At a certain point Filianore fell into a deep sleep hugging a Vagrant egg, causing the appearance of a space-time barrier that isolated the Ringed City from the effects of the fading of the First Flame on the rest of the world. The order of the Spears of the Church was thus founded, which enlisted knights with the duty of protecting the princess's slumber from trespassers, and maintaining the city's state of isolation and containing the Dark Soul within.

claims.text: Slave Knight Gael sought the blood of the Dark Soul as pigment for the Painted World, knowing he was no Champion, that the Dark Soul would likely ruin him and that he had little hope of a safe return.
claims.quote: The red-hooded, wandering slave knight Gael sought the blood of the dark soul as pigment for the Painted World. But Gael knew he was no Champion, that the dark soul would likely ruin him and that he had little hope of a safe return.

claims.text: After the Ashen One finds the Ringed City, the Painter waits for a pigment colored like the dark soul of man; the Blood of the Dark Soul is received after Gael's death and consists of the dark souls consumed by Gael, with blood seeping from his body.
claims.quote: After the Ashen One finds The Ringed City, the Painter mentions that she is waiting to receive a pigment colored like the dark soul of man. It is the Blood of the Dark Soul, received after Gael's death by the Ashen One's hands. The pigment consists of dark souls consumed by Gael, with blood seeping from his body.

claims.text: The Painter is a young woman with draconic lineage whose mother imparted advanced knowledge about the First Flame and the Dark Soul, and harnessing those two primordial forces she has the ability to create new Painted Worlds.
claims.quote: The Painter is a young woman with draconic lineage. Albeit not receiving a name at birth, her mother imparted to her advanced knowledge about the First Flame and the Dark Soul. Harnessing these two primordial forces, she has the ability to create new Painted Worlds.

claims.text: After receiving the pigment, the Painter thanks the Ashen One and, now in possession of Flame and Dark, finally starts work on her painting, continuing to await uncle Gael's return unaware of his death.
claims.quote: After the Painter receives the pigment, she gently thanks the Ashen One and, now in possession of Flame and Dark, she finally starts work on her painting. She continues to await uncle Gael's return, unaware of his death.

q100.question: What are the main differences between the endings of Dark Souls, Dark Souls II, and Dark Souls III, and how does each ending treat the cycle of Fire and Dark?
q100.answer: Each game frames the same choice between prolonging Fire and letting Dark come, but the tone and mechanics of the endings differ. In Dark Souls, the Age of Fire first began after Gwyn and the Lords defeated the Everlasting Dragons and was unnaturally prolonged when Gwyn sacrificed himself to kindle the First Flame; if the Chosen Undead kindles the Flame after defeating Gwyn, they sacrifice themselves as Gwyn did and delay the Age of Dark again, a routine that repeats for generations. Alternatively, abandoning the First Flame to die out after Gwyn's defeat ushers in the Age of Dark, the age of men, and makes the Chosen Undead the fabled Dark Lord; the Age of Dark begins when the First Flame fades completely, ending the Age of Fire and the rule of the gods, and while the sun is extinguished and the world is enveloped in darkness, the Dark Soul of humanity can produce everlasting cold flames and light. Dark Souls II offers two endings at the Throne of Want: proceeding to the throne accepts the Bearer's part in the cycle, either sacrificing themselves to link the flame or allowing it to keep fading and becoming the Dark Lord (the game leaves the choice unknown), while leaving the throne rejects it and has the Bearer walk away bitterly to seek a more permanent end to the curse. The Throne of Want serves to link the First Flame like the thrones of Lothric's Firelink Shrine, and Vendrick refused to sit on it after discovering that linking the flame only makes it fade and the curse return. In Dark Souls III, linking the Fire has the Ashen One burn but the fire is not rekindled, leaving them sitting beside the flame unable to prolong its life as the sun remains a Darksign. The End of Fire, available after giving the Fire Keeper the Eyes of a Fire Keeper, has her take the First Flame; the fire fades, Dark settles, and she predicts that one day tiny flames will dance across the darkness like embers linked by lords past. In Ash Seeketh Embers, the Ashen One strikes down the Fire Keeper before the flames fade and takes the First Flame to offer to the Darksign Sun. The Usurpation of Fire, requiring Yoel to draw out the Ashen One's true strength and Anri to be married, has the Ashen One absorb the fire and awaken before a white Darksign Sun, greeted as Lord by Yuria, Anri and an army of hollows. Dark Souls III also shows that the prolonged Age of Fire has become unsustainable: Prince Lothric rejected prolonging it, the resurrected Lords of Cinder refused their thrones, and the world had become irreparably corrupted with all lands converging on Lothric.

claims.text: The Age of Fire first began after Gwyn and the other Lords defeated the Everlasting Dragons, ending the Age of Ancients, and was unnaturally prolonged when Gwyn sacrificed himself to kindle the First Flame.
claims.quote: The Age of Fire first began after Gwyn and the other Lords defeated the Everlasting Dragons which ended the Age of Ancients. The Age of Fire was unnaturally prolonged when Gwyn sacrificed himself to kindle the First Flame.

claims.text: If the Chosen Undead kindles the First Flame upon Gwyn's defeat, they sacrifice themselves as Gwyn did and delay the Age of Dark once more, a routine repeated for generations.
claims.quote:
When the Chosen Undead talks to Kingseeker Frampt, he will tell them that they are destined to succeed Gwyn. Should the player choose to kindle the First Flame upon the defeat of Gwyn, they will sacrifice themselves as Gwyn did, thus delaying the Age of Dark once more.

Such a routine of kindling the First Flame repeats itself for generations to come, until the time of Prince Lothric, when the prolonging of the fire proves futile.

claims.text: According to Darkstalker Kaathe, should the Chosen Undead abandon the First Flame to die out after defeating Gwyn, they will usher in the Age of Dark and become the fabled Dark Lord.
claims.quote: According to Darkstalker Kaathe, the Chosen Undead, protagonist of *Dark Souls*, is destined to bring about the Age of Dark, as they are the descendant of the Furtive Pygmy, who possessed the Dark Soul and divided it among early humans in the form of Humanity. Should the Chosen Undead abandon the First Flame to die out after the defeat of Gwyn, Lord of Cinder, they will "usher in the Age of Dark", and become the fabled "Dark Lord" of whom Kaathe speaks.

claims.text: In the Age of Dark, the sun itself is extinguished along with the First Flame and the world is enveloped in total darkness, although the Dark Soul of humanity itself is capable of producing everlasting cold flames and light sources.
claims.quote: In the Age of Dark, the sun itself, which is connected to the status of the First Flame, is extinguished along with the Flame, and the world is enveloped in total darkness. However, it is not necessarily an existence completely devoid of fire and illumination as it might seem, as the Dark Soul of humanity itself is capable of producing everlasting flames, even if cold and generating light sources.

claims.text: In Dark Souls II, proceeding to the Throne means the Bearer of the Curse accepts their part in the cycle, either sacrificing themselves to link the flame or allowing it to continue fading and becoming the Dark Lord, with the choice unknown; leaving the throne rejects it and has the Bearer walk away to seek a more permanent way to end the curse.
claims.quote:
***Proceed to the Throne:** In this ending, the Bearer of the Curse will accept their part in the cycle of the world, and take the throne. Doing so means that they will either sacrifice themselves to link the flame, or allow the flame to continue fading and become the Dark Lord. Which the Bearer of the Curse chooses is unknown.

***Leave the Throne: **In this ending, the Bearer of the Curse rejects the throne, and bitterly walks away, seemingly to seek another, more permanent way to end the curse.

claims.text: The Throne of Want serves as a means to link the First Flame, in a way similar to the thrones of Lothric's Firelink Shrine, being built inside a kiln with ashes indicating the remains of previous Lords of Cinder.
claims.quote: The Throne of Want serves as a means to link the First Flame, in a way similar to the thrones of Lothrics’s Firelink Shrine, as it is built inside a kiln and the ashes that cover it seems to indicate the remains of previous Lords of Cinder.

claims.text: Vendrick initially sought to link the fire believing it could end the Undead Curse, but discovered that the flame would fade again and the curse return every time, so he refused to sit on the Throne and sought a permanent way to end the curse.
claims.quote: According to Vendrick and Nashandra, once Vendrick sougth the fire, for he believed that by linking it he could end the Undead Curse. But he would later discover that this was a lie, since the flame would fade again and the curse return every time, he then refused to sit on the Throne and decided to search for a permanent way to end the curse.

claims.text: In Dark Souls III's Link the Fire ending, the Ashen One attempts to link the fire as all the other lords had, but the fire is not rekindled; the Ashen One merely sits beside the flame, unable to prolong its life, as the sun remains a Darksign.
claims.quote: ***Link the Fire**: In this ending, the Ashen One attempts to do as all the other lords had done before them and link the fire. The Ashen One stretches out a hand and begins to burn, but unlike in the past, the fire is not rekindled. Instead, the Ashen One merely sits beside the flame, unable to prolong its life, as the sun remains a Darksign.

claims.text: In The End of Fire ending, after receiving the Eyes of a Fire Keeper, the Fire Keeper takes the First Flame and it fades as dark settles, but she predicts that one day tiny flames will dance across the darkness, like embers linked by lords past.
claims.quote: ***The End of Fire**: If the Ashen One gave the Eyes of a Fire Keeper to the Fire Keeper, they may summon her upon defeating the Soul of Cinder. The Fire Keeper will take the First Flame into her hands. She states that the fire quickly fades and that dark will soon settle, but predicts that one day, tiny flames will dance across the darkness, like embers linked by lords past, suggesting that the other Lords of Cinder of the past will one day rise and wander through the darkness with their own fragments of the First Flame.

claims.text: In the Ash Seeketh Embers ending, the Ashen One strikes down the Fire Keeper before the flames fade and takes the First Flame into their own hands, raising it to offer to the Darksign Sun.
claims.quote: ***Ash Seeketh Embers**: If the Ashen One gave the Eyes of a Fire Keeper to the Fire Keeper, they may summon her upon defeating the Soul of Cinder. The Fire Keeper will take the First Flame into her hands. Before the flames fade, the Ashen One may strike her down. The Ashen One steps over the limp body of the Fire Keeper and takes the First Flame into their own hands. Kneeling, the Ashen One raises the flame, offering it to the Darksign Sun.

claims.text: In The Usurpation of Fire ending, after Yoel draws out the Ashen One's true strength and the Ashen One follows Yuria's instructions and marries Anri, the Ashen One absorbs the fire, collapses, and awakens before a white Darksign Sun, greeted as Lord by Yuria, Anri and an army of hollows.
claims.quote: ***The Usurpation of Fire**: If the Ashen One allowed Yoel to draw out their true strength a sufficient amount of times through the Dark Sigil, followed Yuria's instructions and "married" Anri, the Ashen One may, instead of linking the fire, absorb it into themselves. The Ashen One collapses from the strain and awakens before a Darksign Sun turned white, and also finds Yuria, Anri, and an army of hollows greeting them as their Lord and praying for the Ashen One to make Londor whole.

claims.text: By the time of Dark Souls III the prolonged Age of Fire is failing: Prince Lothric rejected prolonging it, the resurrected Lords of Cinder refused to sit on their thrones, and the material world had become irreparably corrupted with all lands converging on Lothric.
claims.quote: Eventually the one anointed to next link the Flame (and indeed, who was born for that very purpose), Prince Lothric, rejected the idea that the Age of Fire should be prolonged any further and instead desired to end what he called the "fire-linking curse." A contingency plan was then activated, in which previous Lords of Cinder were resurrected in hopes that they, who had linked the First Flame before, might do so again. However, by this time, the world that had been created during the Age of Fire had become a twisted shadow of its former self. As a result of the prolonging of the current Age, the act of which seemingly constituted a rejection of the natural order, the material world had become irreparably corrupted, and all lands from all previous points in time had begun to converge upon a single point: the Kingdom of Lothric. Upon reviving and seeing what had become of the world they had fought to protect, the Lords of Cinder, too, rejected the linking of the Flame and refused to sit upon their thrones.
